title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics
book_title: Chapter 3: The Economics of Small-Molecule Monopolies vs. Bespoke Cell Therapy

epigraph.quote: Gross margin is where biology meets manufacturing; operating margin is where biology meets distribution.
epigraph.author: Specialty Pharma Unit-Economics Maxim

web_blocks.html: Vertex's unit economics show a sharp split between its legacy CF pills and its newer drugs [1, 2, 10]. In Cystic Fibrosis, Vertex relies on highly concentrated distribution: in FY2025, just two customers—McKesson Corporation (22% of total revenue, 19% of AR) and Accredo Health Group (12% of total revenue)—accounted for 34% of consolidated revenue, alongside Lloyds Pharmacy at 10% of AR [1]. U.S. sales hit $2.17 billion in Q3 2026 [5]. Abroad, government-backed supply deals drove $1.27 billion in Q3 2026 [5]. Because CF care centers on ~130+ U.S. CF Foundation clinics and European national registries, Vertex needs a very lean sales team [13]. In FY2025, total Cost of Sales was $1,651.3 million on $12,001.3 million of revenue [1]. That yielded an 86.2% GAAP gross margin, even after tiered CFF royalties and Casgevy's early plant ramp [1, 13].

Supply chain needs differ sharply across Vertex's newer pillars. For Casgevy, Vertex does not ship vials to wholesalers [10]. Instead, it runs a custom vein-to-vein cold chain for each patient [10]. Doctors collect stem cells at an Authorized Treatment Center (ATC) and ship them under strict tracking to cleanrooms like Lonza and RoslinCT [10]. There, teams edit the cells with CRISPR/Cas9 and run multi-week quality checks [10]. The cells return to the ATC only after the patient finishes busulfan chemo [10]. Each ATC needs hospital accreditation, transplant beds, and specialist staff [10, 15]. That setup creates a hard capacity limit on how fast Casgevy can scale, even with strong demand [10, 15]. Net profits and losses for Casgevy under the CRISPR Therapeutics collaboration are split 60% Vertex / 40% CRISPR, while Vertex also depends on Lonza for T1D cell-therapy manufacturing and third-party CMOs for povetacicept [1].

Journavx (suzetrigine) brings the exact opposite hurdle: broad retail and hospital access [11]. Unlike CF or SCD, acute pain spans thousands of hospitals, surgery centers, and retail pharmacies. To reach them, Vertex grew SG&A from $1,137.0 million in FY2023 to $1,464.3 million in FY2024 and $1,753.1 million in FY2025 [1, 14]. That spend built a wide hospital and retail sales force [4, 11]. Vertex also had to win Medicare Part D and commercial PBM coverage while fighting step-therapy rules tied to cheap generic opioids and NSAIDs [4, 11]. By contrast, Palsonify (acromegaly) fits right back into Vertex's lean rare-disease pharmacy model at focused endocrine clinics [6].

web_blocks.caption: FY2025 Per-$100 Revenue & Cash-Flow Waterfall ($12,001.3M Audited Base)
web_blocks.takeaway: Out of every $100 of FY2025 revenue, Vertex retained $86.24 after COGS, reinvested $32.58 in R&D, absorbed $3.16 in VX-264 impairment, generated $34.77 in GAAP EBIT, earned $32.94 in GAAP Net Income, and converted $26.61 into Free Cash Flow [1, 14].

web_blocks.html: The FY2025 waterfall shows the huge profit engine beneath Vertex's R&D budget [1]. In FY2025, Vertex spent $3,909.5 million on R&D (32.6% of revenue) and $1,753.1 million on SG&A (14.6% of revenue) to launch five franchises at once [1]. Even with that heavy spend, it turned 34.8% of revenue into GAAP operating income ($4,173.0 million) and 26.6% into free cash flow ($3,193.0 million) [1, 14]. Capital needs stay very low. FY2025 CapEx of $438.0 million was just 3.6% of revenue, since small-molecule pill output scales with little new plant spend [1]. In Q3 2026, full-year combined GAAP R&D, AIPR&D, and SG&A guidance jumped to $7.15–$7.20 billion (from $6.30–$6.45 billion), reflecting Crinetics integration, ~$500 million of Crinetics compensation/transaction costs, ~$100 million of AIPR&D, and Journavx/povetacicept launch spend [5].

web_blocks.title: Unit-Economics Watch: Gross Margin Compression & Royalty Shifts
paragraphs: As Casgevy ($99M in Q3 2026) and Palsonify grow, blended gross margin faces a tug-of-war [4, 5, 10]. Custom cell-therapy plants carry higher COGS than small-molecule pills, while Journavx earns a lower net price per script [4, 5, 10].

Mechanically, under the CFF Agreement, sales of combination CF drugs are allocated equally across active ingredients: pre-March 2014 compounds (ivacaftor, lumacaftor, tezacaftor) carry single-digit to sub-teen royalties, March 2014–August 2016 compounds (elexacaftor) carry low-to-mid-single-digit royalties, and post-September 2016 compounds (vanzacaftor, deutivacaftor) carry zero CFF royalty [1]. Thus Trikafta pays on all three APIs, whereas Alyftrek ($706M in Q3 2026) pays only on one-third (tezacaftor), lifting net CF gross margin [1, 5, 9].

web_blocks.takeaway: Vertex's unit economics are strongest in oral rare-disease pills (CF, Palsonify) and most constrained in hospital-bound cell therapy (Casgevy) and rebate-heavy acute pain (Journavx) [1, 5, 6, 10, 11].

book_paragraphs: To see why Vertex's business model is so unusual, follow one hundred dollars of FY2025 revenue as it travels down the income statement and out into the cash flow statement. Out of every $100 Vertex collected from patients and payers in 2025, only $13.76 went to Cost of Sales—leaving $86.24 in gross profit. That is the magic of small-molecule chemistry at scale: once you discover a pill like Trikafta, stamping out another bottle of tablets costs pennies on the dollar.

From that $86.24 of gross profit, Vertex voluntarily ploughed roughly $32.58 right back into Research and Development and another $14.61 into Selling, General, and Administrative expenses. Think about that for a moment. Vertex spends nearly a third of its top line on R&D—a higher reinvestment rate than almost any mega-cap pharmaceutical peer—and yet it still brought $34.77 per $100 down to GAAP operating income. Add in $4.03 per $100 of net interest income earned on its cash pile, subtract $5.75 in taxes, and Vertex kept $32.94 of every $100 in GAAP net income. After just $3.65 in capital expenditures, $26.61 landed in free cash flow.

Why is SG&A so lean—under fifteen percent of sales—for a twelve-billion-dollar drugmaker? Because cystic fibrosis care is concentrated in roughly 130 specialized care centers across the United States and national registries in Europe. Vertex doesn't need an army of ten thousand primary-care sales reps knocking on suburban clinic doors. A small, medically fluent team covers nearly the entire addressable patient population. Yet that concentration cuts both ways on credit and channel risk: per the FY2025 10-K, just two distributors—McKesson Corporation (22% of revenue) and Accredo Health Group (12% of revenue)—represented 34% of Vertex's total revenue, with Lloyds Pharmacy accounting for 10% of accounts receivable.

That distribution advantage is precisely what gets tested as Vertex moves outside cystic fibrosis. Casgevy requires an intricate hospital-based vein-to-vein cold chain at Authorized Treatment Centers, with weeks of cell editing and inpatient chemotherapy. Journavx, by contrast, has to fight for formulary placement in retail pharmacies and surgical centers against dirt-cheap generic painkillers. Both can succeed, but neither enjoys the effortless distribution economics of Trikafta and Alyftrek.

Notice how sharply Vertex's distribution economics differ across its product lines. In cystic fibrosis, a small team of specialist account managers supports accredited CF care centers, while specialty pharmacies handle prior authorizations and patient adherence. Once a patient starts Trikafta or Alyftrek, refill rates remain remarkably sticky for decades, keeping selling, general, and administrative costs near 14.6% of revenue.

By contrast, Casgevy requires a bespoke, patient-specific autologous supply chain inside Authorized Treatment Centers, with months of apheresis, CRISPR editing, quality release, and busulfan conditioning between cell collection and revenue recognition. Journavx requires a completely different muscle: hospital formulary committees, ambulatory surgery centers, and retail pharmacy contracting. Managing all three distribution models simultaneously without letting SG&A bloat is one of management's defining operational tests.

book_callouts.title: Gross Margin Is Only Half the Story
book_callouts.text: High gross margins mean little if you have to spend forty percent of revenue on sales reps to move the product. Vertex's real superpower in cystic fibrosis is the combination of an 86% gross margin and a 15% SG&A ratio—a rare pairing that turns specialized science into a 27% free-cash-flow margin.

book_subsections.title: The Alyftrek Royalty Arbitrage & Working Capital Discipline
paragraphs: One subtle unit-economics lever deserves your attention: Cystic Fibrosis Foundation (CFF) royalties. Under the amended CFF Agreement, combination-product net sales are allocated equally across each active pharmaceutical ingredient. Pre-March 2014 molecules (ivacaftor, lumacaftor, tezacaftor) carry tiered single-digit to sub-teen royalties, elexacaftor carries low-to-mid-single digits, and compounds synthesized after September 1, 2016 (vanzacaftor and deutivacaftor) carry zero CFF royalty. That means Trikafta pays royalties on all three components, whereas once-daily Alyftrek pays only on its one-third tezacaftor share—dropping substantial royalty savings straight to gross margin.

Working capital is equally clean. In FY2025, Vertex generated $3.63 billion in operating cash flow against $3.95 billion in net income, a ninety-two percent cash conversion ratio. Receivables turn briskly because specialty-pharmacy distributors and national health systems pay reliably, and inventory builds are modest outside of cell-therapy raw materials. As we look at the balance sheet later, keep in mind that this low-capex, high-conversion core is what allowed Vertex to absorb billions in M&A without breaking stride.

book_subsections.title: Why Payer Friction and Hospital Capacity Matter More Than Manufacturing
paragraphs: When investors study pharmaceutical supply chains, they often worry about factory bottlenecks or active-ingredient shortages. For Vertex in 2026, the real bottlenecks sit downstream in hospital beds and insurance formularies. Take Casgevy: even if Vertex's contract manufacturers can edit twice as many stem-cell batches tomorrow, a hospital Authorized Treatment Center still has to schedule apheresis, reserve an inpatient bone-marrow-transplant bed for weeks of busulfan recovery, and secure single-case payer sign-off. That physical and administrative queue sets a natural speed limit on Casgevy's revenue curve.

Journavx faces the opposite bottleneck: pharmacy benefit managers. Because generic ibuprofen and generic oxycodone cost pennies per dose, insurers throw up prior-authorization walls and step-therapy requirements before paying for a branded non-opioid pill. That is why Vertex's SG&A jumped from $1.14 billion in 2023 to $1.75 billion in 2025—it takes real commercial muscle to win formulary tiering across thousands of hospitals and plans. By contrast, Palsonify in acromegaly and povetacicept in IgA nephropathy plug straight back into concentrated specialist networks where Vertex's lean rare-disease model shines.

book_subsections.title: Tracing Every $100 of Revenue Down to Free Cash Flow
paragraphs: Look at our FY2025 $100 revenue-to-free-cash-flow waterfall: out of every $100 Vertex collects at the top line, only $13.76 goes to cost of goods sold and royalties, leaving $86.24 in gross profit. Vertex then reinvests $32.58 of every $100 back into research and development, $14.61 into selling, general, and administrative expenses, $1.11 into acquired IPR&D, and $3.16 into the Q1 2025 VX-264 intangible impairment charge ($379.0 million), leaving $34.77 in GAAP operating profit (with $1.75 of D&A backed out of operating expenses so nothing is double-counted).

Add $4.03 in net non-operating income ($4.09 gross interest income less $0.06 other expense), subtract $0.11 in interest expense and $5.75 in taxes, and Vertex earns $32.94 in GAAP net income—converting $30.26 of every $100 into operating cash flow and $26.61 into pure free cash flow after $3.65 in capital expenditures.
